messages.content: Respond to a fictional educational clinical case for a research evaluation. Follow the stated task and audience. Use only the supplied patient facts and conversation. Distinguish facts from hypotheses and make uncertainty explicit. Give concise final clinical justifications, not a private internal reasoning trace.

Case facts:
Basic patient information: 58-year-old woman.
Only existing selected records are available. Unreported information remains unknown, not normal, negative or evidence that a test was never performed. Do not infer an exact test/report time when none is given. Later diagnoses and outcomes are withheld.
Patient opening:
I do not remember the night-time events and feel normal again in the morning.

Task:
Write 150–220 words in plain English for the patient and her family. This is a review of the recorded episodes, not a live episode. Answer: “What might explain these night-time episodes, what do any investigation results obtained tell us, and what should we do next?” Explain the relevance of any glucose measurements obtained without claiming a final cause, describe why further assessment is needed, and include what to do if a severe episode recurs. Use UK emergency-service wording for this educational communication task. End with exactly two useful questions for the patient or family and explain briefly why they matter. Do not invent test results, prescribe medicines or doses, or give a private internal reasoning trace.

Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.

Earlier conversation (context):
Clinician: Can you describe what happens during these night-time events? For example, do you move, make sounds, or do others notice anything unusual?
Patient: I have lost about 5 kg and have less energy and more difficulty concentrating.
Fixed collateral record [Six-month night-time episode history; no exact event dates supplied.]: She shouts, makes purposeless movements and thrashes in bed, sometimes with urinary incontinence.
Fixed collateral record [Six-month night-time episode history; no exact event dates supplied.]: Her family cannot easily wake her, and she cannot remember the events.

Clinician: Have you ever had similar episodes during the day, or any episodes where you lost awareness, had unusual movements, or felt a strange sensation beforehand? Also, do you have any known neurological conditions or a history of head injury?
Patient: I was diagnosed with moderate obstructive sleep apnoea one month ago, and it has not been treated. I have no history of diabetes.

Clinician: Have you had any brain imaging (CT or MRI) or an EEG performed, either for these episodes or for the sleep apnoea work-up? If so, could you share the results?
Fixed clinical record [Existing EEG; precise recording time is not supplied.]: An electroencephalogram (EEG) showed no definite epileptiform discharges.

Clinician: Have you had any brain imaging, such as a CT scan or MRI, performed? If so, what were the findings?
Simulator: No additional recorded detail is available for this question. This is not a negative finding or proof that a test was never performed.
Controller: No new recorded information was returned. Do not repeat this request; change the question or finish. This is not a negative finding.

Clinician: Are you currently taking any medications or supplements, and have you noticed any other changes in your health over the past few months, such as changes in appetite, sleep, mood, or any new symptoms like headaches or visual changes?
Patient: I take irbesartan for high blood pressure.

message.content:
Review of your night-time episodes

Your episodes, including shouting, thrashing, and sometimes wetting the bed, with no memory the next morning, could be explained by several things. Your untreated moderate obstructive sleep apnoea is one possibility, as severe oxygen drops during sleep can trigger unusual movements and confusion. Nocturnal seizures are another consideration, though your EEG did not show definite epileptiform discharges, which is reassuring but does not fully exclude them. Nocturnal low blood sugar is a further possibility; no glucose measurements are on record, so an overnight glucose check would help rule this out.

Your weight loss, reduced energy, and difficulty concentrating are concerning and need further investigation. We would recommend a sleep study to assess your apnoea treatment needs, a repeat EEG if episodes continue, and blood tests including glucose. Brain imaging has not been recorded as performed, and this may be considered.

If a severe episode recurs, with prolonged confusion, repeated convulsions, or injury, call 999 and say you are having a possible seizure or medical emergency.

Two questions for you:

Has anyone witnessed an episode where your eyes rolled or your body stiffened? This helps distinguish seizure from other causes.

Do you snore loudly or stop breathing during sleep, as noted by a partner? This confirms the severity of your apnoea and guides urgent treatment.
